scenes.tts: A newborn ferret's eyes have not opened yet. Even so, its retina is firing.
scenes.visual: Title card: Timing Is the Address. A flat retina in the dark; a few ganglion cells flicker.
scenes.narration: A newborn ferret's eyes have not opened yet. Even so, its retina is firing.

scenes.tts: Its ganglion cells fire bursts that sweep across the tissue as waves.
scenes.visual: A wave front sweeps across the flat retina; ganglion cells light as it passes. Label: ganglion cells, the retina's output neurons.
scenes.narration: Its ganglion cells fire bursts that sweep across the tissue as waves.

scenes.tts: Nothing is being seen. Why send this to the brain?
scenes.visual: The retina goes dark. Label: a minute or two of silence. A question mark over the optic nerve heading to the brain.
scenes.narration: Nothing is being seen. Why send this to the brain?

scenes.tts: The brain is still wiring itself. Molecules have drawn only a rough first map.
scenes.visual: Axons from the retina reach the thalamus roughly in order, guided by a colour gradient. Label: Eph and ephrin gradients, a rough first map.
scenes.narration: The brain is still wiring itself. Molecules have drawn only a rough first map.

scenes.tts: In the thalamus, the two eyes' axons at first overlap. Later they separate.
scenes.visual: LGN outline. Left-eye axons in one colour, right-eye in another, intermixed; then a later panel with separate layers. Labels: early, overlap; adult, separate.
scenes.narration: In the thalamus, the two eyes' axons at first overlap. Later they separate.

scenes.tts: Two cells side by side in one eye sit at almost the same point on the gradients.
scenes.visual: Two ganglion cells 20 micrometres apart in one retina, with the gradient bar beneath them; both point to nearly the same value.
scenes.narration: Two cells side by side in one eye sit at almost the same point on the gradients.

scenes.tts: So does a cell at the matching point in the other eye, though molecular cues also differ somewhat between the eyes. It still has to end up in a different territory, and the cues alone do not finish the job.
scenes.visual: A second retina for the other eye; a third cell at the matching point, on nearly the same gradient value, with a small separate tag marking its eye. Then the adult LGN: the two neighbours side by side, the third cell's axon in the other eye's territory.
scenes.narration: So does a cell at the matching point in the other eye, though molecular cues also differ somewhat between the eyes. It still has to end up in a different territory, and the cues alone do not finish the job.

scenes.tts: Timing can sort them. Watch a wave cross the retina at about one hundred micrometres a second.
scenes.caption: Timing can sort them. Watch a wave cross the retina at about 100 micrometres a second.
scenes.visual: A wave front crosses the first retina. On screen: about 100 micrometres per second; bursts of a few seconds, take 2 s.
scenes.narration: Timing can sort them. Watch a wave cross the retina at about 100 micrometres a second.

scenes.tts: Two cells this close fire almost together. Their bursts overlap almost completely.
scenes.visual: Spike rasters for the two neighbouring cells stacked. On screen: 20 micrometres apart, 0.2 s apart, 2 s bursts; overlap (2 − 0.2) ÷ 2 = 90 percent.
scenes.narration: Two cells this close fire almost together. Their bursts overlap almost completely.

scenes.tts: A cell a millimetre farther along the wave's path fires ten seconds later. Their bursts do not overlap.
scenes.visual: A third raster for a cell 1,000 micrometres farther along the same wave's path, with an arrow showing the one wave direction. On screen: 1,000 µm ÷ 100 µm/s = 10 s; no overlap. A note: along this path, overlap ends by 200 micrometres.
scenes.narration: A cell a millimetre farther along the wave's path fires ten seconds later. Their bursts do not overlap.

scenes.tts: Now predict. What about a cell at the same point in the other eye?
scenes.visual: The other eye's retina beside the first, its cell highlighted, raster row empty with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Now predict. What about a cell at the same point in the other eye?

scenes.tts: Its waves are not timed to this eye's, so it matches only by chance, a few percent of the time.
scenes.visual: The other eye's raster fills in with bursts at unrelated times; an occasional chance overlap is circled. On screen: by chance, a few percent.
scenes.narration: Its waves are not timed to this eye's, so it matches only by chance, a few percent of the time.

scenes.tts: But waves start in many places and run in varying directions.
scenes.visual: Several waves start at different places on the retina and travel in varying directions, some directions a little more often than others.
scenes.narration: But waves start in many places and run in varying directions.

scenes.tts: So position is carried not by one cell's timing, but by how closely two cells' firing matches, over many waves.
scenes.visual: One cell's spike times alone, scattered and meaningless; then a plot of match between two cells against distance apart, high near zero and fading smoothly with distance, with no sharp edge.
scenes.narration: So position is carried not by one cell's timing, but by how closely two cells' firing matches, over many waves.

scenes.tts: How could a target cell use that match? In nineteen forty-nine, the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed a rule.
scenes.caption: How could a target cell use that match? In 1949, the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed a rule.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Donald Hebb, 1949. Two cells, A and B, with an axon from A to B.
scenes.narration: How could a target cell use that match? In 1949, the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed a rule.

scenes.tts: In paraphrase: when cell A repeatedly takes part in firing cell B, A becomes more effective at firing B.
scenes.visual: A fires, B fires, the A to B synapse thickens. Label: Hebb's rule, in paraphrase.
scenes.narration: In paraphrase: when cell A repeatedly takes part in firing cell B, A becomes more effective at firing B.

scenes.tts: Take one thalamic cell with inputs from both eyes, each firing in its own waves. Predict: what happens to the right eye's inputs?
scenes.visual: An LGN cell with two clusters of synapses, left-eye and right-eye, each cluster lighting in its own waves. Question: what happens to the right-eye inputs?
scenes.narration: Take one thalamic cell with inputs from both eyes, each firing in its own waves. Predict: what happens to the right eye's inputs?

scenes.tts: If they are strong enough to fire the cell at their own times, they strengthen too. Hebb's rule only strengthens, so the cell stays binocular.
scenes.visual: Both synapse clusters thicken. Label: Hebb alone, everything strengthens.
scenes.narration: If they are strong enough to fire the cell at their own times, they strengthen too. Hebb's rule only strengthens, so the cell stays binocular.

scenes.tts: Segregation needs a second half: competition.
scenes.visual: The cell is shown still wired to both eyes. A heading appears: the missing half, competition.
scenes.narration: Segregation needs a second half: competition.

scenes.tts: Picture the inputs sharing a fixed budget. Each round, both eyes grow, then the same amount is taken back from each.
scenes.visual: A fixed-size budget bar under the synapses, split between left and right. Label: toy model, equal amounts taken back each round.
scenes.narration: Picture the inputs sharing a fixed budget. Each round, both eyes grow, then the same amount is taken back from each.

scenes.tts: The eye that starts slightly ahead gains more than it gives back. So it pulls further ahead.
scenes.visual: The bar starts 5.5 to 4.5, then 5.6 to 4.4, then 5.72 to 4.28; the left share keeps growing. Label: a toy model, not a measurement.
scenes.narration: The eye that starts slightly ahead gains more than it gives back. So it pulls further ahead.

scenes.tts: In this toy model, the other eye's inputs are pushed out of that cell.
scenes.visual: The right-eye synapses thin and retract; the cell is now driven by one eye. Label: toy model, growth of 20 percent of each eye's own strength, then 1 unit taken back from each.
scenes.narration: In this toy model, the other eye's inputs are pushed out of that cell.

scenes.tts: Rescale both eyes in proportion instead, and the split never changes. The kind of sharing matters.
scenes.visual: Side panel: the same bar rescaled in proportion stays at 5.5 to 4.5 round after round. Label: proportional rescaling, no winner.
scenes.narration: Rescale both eyes in proportion instead, and the split never changes. The kind of sharing matters.

scenes.tts: Takeaway: timing is the address. A cell keeps inputs that fire in step with its strong inputs, and they crowd out the rest.
scenes.visual: Guiding idea on screen: Timing is the address. A target cell keeps the inputs that fire in step with its other strong inputs, and because the inputs compete, the ones it keeps crowd out the rest.
scenes.narration: Takeaway: timing is the address. A cell keeps inputs that fire in step with its strong inputs, and they crowd out the rest.
